## Summary

The speakers argue that the published link between the acute chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and injury may be a statistical artifact of the training schedule. A hard recent week makes a hard session today more likely, and the intensity of that session is what raises injury risk. They simulated seasons from NFL and Italian soccer load data in which only same-session intensity affected injury, and the ACWR still looked strongly predictive. When session load is accounted for, ACWR loses significance in their data. They say this does not prove the earlier papers wrong. It matters because the metric underpins software and consulting products sold as injury prevention.

## Key claims

- The first speaker says a vendor once claimed it could cut injury rates by over 50%, and he calls that claim false; he is generally skeptical of injury-prevention products. [00:30]
- ACWR is the last 7 days of load divided by the last 28 days, and it has been applied to many load types, including perceived exertion, heart rate, GPS, accelerometer data and minutes played. [04:35]
- The literature proposes a U-shaped relationship with injury and a "sweet spot" of lower risk. [05:05]
- Positives named for ACWR: easy to calculate, intuitive for coaches, and it pushes coaches to consider past training and not only today. [05:36]
- The speakers say critics had already raised other problems: exponentially weighted versions, mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, weak out-of-sample prediction, and no data in the offseason. [08:09]
- The speakers' hunch was that ACWR is an artifact of the training schedule, because training camp has both the highest load and the highest injury risk. [09:39]
- Prior studies calculate ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session; they find a strong relationship across sports. [10:40]
- The proposed causal structure: schedule drives both ACWR and session intensity, and session intensity drives injury. A hard prior week predicts a hard upcoming session. [11:41]
- In the speakers' own data, ACWR is highly predictive of injury in a given session. [13:12]
- In simulations where ACWR had no effect by construction, ACWR still came out extremely significant on a chi-square test. [14:13]
- The apparent injury-risk increase in the simulations was about the same order as the literature reports. [15:15]
- Sessions in the "danger zone" of ACWR were more likely to be hard sessions. [16:16]
- A suggested fix is to use the actual session load of the session in which injury occurred, for example with survival models, latent variable models, or other players' loads in the same session. [17:49]
- Prior studies have not used same-session load because the data for an injured player is usually discarded. [17:18]
- Once session load is accounted for, ACWR goes from highly significant to non-significant in all their cases. [18:19]
- The speakers say they have not disproved the field, only shown the analysis is open to confounding; a more complex model might still find real signal. [18:49] [23:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- ACWR: acute load (most recent 7 days) divided by chronic load (previous 28 days). [04:04]
- Sweet spot: captions read "08 and 1.3", almost certainly 0.8 to 1.3, but the captions do not confirm it. [05:36]
- 2014 first paper (cricket bowlers) cited over 250 times; the 2015 editorial (captions: "blanch and gabbit") cited over 150 times. [07:38]
- Uncoupled ACWR: most recent 7 days over the 28 days before those 7 days. [08:39]
- Data: one NFL team and one Italian soccer team (captions say "Syria" and "Serria", likely Serie A; not confirmed). [12:11]
- Simulation: 1,000 simulated seasons per sport, injury probability depends only on the current session's intensity. [13:43]
- Post-simulation apparent risk increase: 6.8% for the Italian team, 10.5% for the NFL team. The talk does not say whether these are relative or absolute. [15:15]
- Injury definition (Q&A): non-contact injury causing the player to miss a subsequent session or match, in line with the UEFA definition. [20:22] [20:53]
- The 6.8% and 10.5% figures are read from auto captions; they were not checked against the slides.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Directed acyclic graph of ACWR, schedule, session intensity and injury. [11:10]
- Null-model simulation: simulate season-by-season session injuries where only session load matters, then test ACWR against injury with a chi-square test. [13:43] [14:43]
- Adjustment options: survival models, latent variable models, or predicting the upcoming session load as an unmeasured confounder. [18:19] [25:11]
- Comparison of coupled and uncoupled ACWR denominators, same result. [26:42]

## Limits and open questions

- Two teams from two sports; no detail on roster size, number of injuries, or load metric used.
- Details of the real-data adjustment models are "in the paper" and were not shown. [17:49]
- The talk does not show the adjusted effect sizes, only that significance disappears.
- Whether chronic load is protective is explicitly not addressed. [26:42]
- Whether a richer multivariate model finds signal is left open. [23:35]
- The claim that better sensors would make the problem worse is the speaker's intuition, not a test. [21:54]
- The speakers' view that ACWR products are "snake oil" is their own opinion, stated early in the talk. [01:01]
- Wellness questionnaire data: one speaker says across four sports the players mostly enter the same value (captions: "seven") every day. This is his experience, not a study. [24:39]
- Minor inconsistency: the talk opens strongly against the industry but closes saying it has not disproved the literature. [18:49]

## Q&A

- How is injury defined, and are non-training injuries dropped? Non-contact injuries causing a missed session or match; cannot rule out training relation for off-field injuries. [20:22]
- Do device sensitivity limits matter? Noise in load sensors should weaken the effect, so the speaker expects better data not to remove the problem. [21:23]
- How should decision makers avoid snake oil? Much sport science is well supported (nutrition, strength and conditioning); this may not be one of them. [22:33]
- Could wellness, physiological and biomarker data in a multivariate model do better? Possibly; dose is measurable, response is not well measured, and wellness forms lack validation. [23:35] [24:39]
- Can you predict today's load from the prior 7 days? If so, treat it as an unmeasured confounder and adjust; needs statistical skill. [25:11]
- Do high vs low chronic loads differ, and is chronic load protective? Same results using acute load alone; protection not addressed; coupled and uncoupled denominators gave the same results. [26:42]

## Where this applies

- Inference: Any Baylor football dashboard that flags players by ACWR on Catapult player load, or by a similar 7-to-28-day ratio, should be treated as a description of recent load and schedule, not as an injury-risk score. Check whether the flags mostly fire on the same weeks (camp, return from breaks) for every player.
- Inference: When reviewing a non-contact injury, pull that day's planned session load (or the practice script intensity) next to the prior-week ratio before attributing it to "spike" in load. The talk's point is that the current session's intensity may carry the signal.
- Inference: For Baylor's own retrospective analysis, log planned session intensity as a field so injured-session data is not lost. The talk says the injured player's session data is usually thrown out. [17:18]
- Inference: Use the simulation idea as a test of any internal risk model: simulate seasons where only session intensity matters and see whether the model still "finds" an ACWR effect.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model such as ACWR is attributed to Eric in the corpus; ACWR appears only in Clemson reference material. The talk neither conflicts with nor changes a stated Baylor position.
- Eric's baseline: Abrupt, large changes in volume and intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver, and progressions are kept smooth (course material, speaker unconfirmed, tagged Inferred). The talk agrees that load change matters but says the ratio may just reflect the schedule; it leaves open whether spikes themselves cause injury.
- Eric's baseline: Subjective daily wellness surveys were abandoned because athletes learned to give consistent low-effort answers (Explicit, SportSmith piece). The talk agrees: a speaker describes athletes entering the same number every day. [24:39]

## What would have to be true

- Session-level load (planned and actual) for every player and session, including the session where an injury occurs.
- A clear non-contact injury definition (the talk uses missed session or match).
- Enough injuries and seasons at Baylor to fit a model that includes session load; the talk does not give a minimum, and one college roster may be too small.
- Someone with the statistical training to run survival or latent variable models. The speaker says this takes "fair bit" of skill. [25:41]

## Do not apply when

- You would use the talk to say ACWR-style monitoring is useless. The speakers say they did not disprove it, and do not show that chronic load is non-protective. [18:49] [26:42]
- Your data has only a handful of injuries; a null result then says little.
- The injury is contact-related; the talk's definition excludes it.
- You want to generalize from one NFL team and one Italian soccer team to a college football roster with different schedules and session structure.
- The claim is being used as settled in a staff meeting. It is a conference research talk; the adjusted results were not shown.

## First step

Export one season of Catapult session load and injury dates for football, and count how many non-contact injuries had a recorded session load for that day. If the count is near zero, fix the logging before any modeling.

## Summary

The speaker, introduced as director of football research and development for the Tennessee Titans, gives a non-technical walk through building an injury-risk model that staff will actually use. She says to model risk, not individual injuries, and that adoption depends on the front office, scouts, medical staff, coaches, strength coaches and players. She lists data sources (tracking, weight room, speed, player surveys, injury history), scheduling choices, model-design issues such as small samples, and delivery through stoplight thresholds and fast alerts. No model results or accuracy numbers are shown. The talk is a practitioner's checklist and opinion, not a validation study.

## Key claims

- The goal is injury risk, not predicting a specific injury, because risk is actionable and a single injury is hard to predict. [01:01]
- Choose which injuries to model; some (bone breaks, cuts) may be excluded and lower-body injuries may be the priority because they cost more time. [01:32]
- Injury matters for team, player and bottom-line reasons; she cites about 13.2 million per NFL team in injury cash last year. [02:33] [03:06]
- A model will not be used if the front office, scouts, medical staff, coaches, strength coaches and players are not invested. [03:36]
- Telling players why they are tested gives better buy-in and better data. [06:38]
- Data sources: tracking (practice and game), weight-room velocity and power, camera-based form, speed analysis, player self-evaluation, and injury history. [07:08]
- NFL rules bar tracking players outside the building, so sleep, hydration, stress and soreness are hard to capture; a survey is one option, with each player using the scale differently. [08:40] [09:12]
- Injury history is called the greatest predictor of future injury. [09:12]
- Test timing changes meaning: Monday after a game is more a fatigue indicator, Wednesday more a readiness indicator. [10:13]
- Frequent testing causes test fatigue; be selective and cut tests that do not help. [10:43]
- She says the NFL needs three injury models: in-season, offseason and training camp. [11:13]
- Outcome choices include games missed, practices missed, soreness, survey responses, or unsupervised anomaly detection. [12:15]
- Sample size is the big challenge; individual-player models need data, so rookies use position, body-size or skill-group models until an onboarding period yields enough data. [13:15] [14:16]
- Evaluating a working model is hard because success means fewer injuries, and injuries are zero-inflated. [14:16] [14:46]
- Outputs must be interpretable to everyone, use stoplight severity levels, and set reasonable expectations because players cannot always sit. [15:49] [16:19]
- Alerts should be immediate: Monday testing goes out Monday night. [17:21]

## Summary

The speakers argue that the published link between the acute chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and injury may be a statistical artifact of the training schedule. A hard recent week makes a hard session today more likely, and the intensity of that session is what raises injury risk. They simulated seasons from NFL and Italian soccer load data in which only same-session intensity affected injury, and the ACWR still looked strongly predictive. When session load is accounted for, ACWR loses significance in their data. They say this does not prove the earlier papers wrong. It matters because the metric underpins software and consulting products sold as injury prevention.

## Key claims

- The first speaker says a vendor once claimed it could cut injury rates by over 50%, and he calls that claim false; he is generally skeptical of injury-prevention products. [00:30]
- ACWR is the last 7 days of load divided by the last 28 days, and it has been applied to many load types, including perceived exertion, heart rate, GPS, accelerometer data and minutes played. [04:35]
- The literature proposes a U-shaped relationship with injury and a "sweet spot" of lower risk. [05:05]
- Positives named for ACWR: easy to calculate, intuitive for coaches, and it pushes coaches to consider past training and not only today. [05:36]
- The speakers say critics had already raised other problems: exponentially weighted versions, mathematical coupling of numerator and denominator, weak out-of-sample prediction, and no data in the offseason. [08:09]
- The speakers' hunch was that ACWR is an artifact of the training schedule, because training camp has both the highest load and the highest injury risk. [09:39]
- Prior studies calculate ACWR going into each session and check whether an injury occurred in that session; they find a strong relationship across sports. [10:40]
- The proposed causal structure: schedule drives both ACWR and session intensity, and session intensity drives injury. A hard prior week predicts a hard upcoming session. [11:41]
- In the speakers' own data, ACWR is highly predictive of injury in a given session. [13:12]
- In simulations where ACWR had no effect by construction, ACWR still came out extremely significant on a chi-square test. [14:13]
- The apparent injury-risk increase in the simulations was about the same order as the literature reports. [15:15]
- Sessions in the "danger zone" of ACWR were more likely to be hard sessions. [16:16]
- A suggested fix is to use the actual session load of the session in which injury occurred, for example with survival models, latent variable models, or other players' loads in the same session. [17:49]
- Prior studies have not used same-session load because the data for an injured player is usually discarded. [17:18]
- Once session load is accounted for, ACWR goes from highly significant to non-significant in all their cases. [18:19]

- Inference: Review "easy day" and walk-through sessions for acceleration and deceleration load, since the talk reports low-key practice often carries more load than staff expect.
- Inference: Give athletes a clear way to see their own data and the reason it is collected, to support buy-in.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost versus insight, and inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data. The talk agrees in asking for validation and reproducibility before use.
- Eric's baseline: recovery has to be earned by training hard, and the field's load-monitoring culture created a "culture of fear" that under-trains athletes. The talk agrees: too little intensity raises game injury risk. [06:10] [52:59]

## What would have to be true

- Catapult session tags that reliably separate practice types (for example walk-through versus team period) so load can be compared with game peaks.

- NBA, cricket or rugby findings are carried straight into college football without checking Baylor's contact rules and practice limits.

## Summary

Phil Wagner, founder of Sparta Science, argues that a standardized vertical jump on a portable force plate can flag injury risk and physical readiness, including upper body injuries in baseball pitchers. He models the approach on medicine: clinical expertise, athlete input and evidence, plus a standardized assessment. The jump is scored on three phases (load, explode, drive) into a "movement signature" with thresholds, and software turns imbalances into a prioritized exercise plan. Injury history, sport load and sleep sit on a dashboard. The talk is a vendor presentation with case studies and claimed results, but no data tables appear in the captions. The Q&A covers balance and landing tests, buy-in, football versus baseball targets and youth use.

## Key claims

- A jump can predict an injury, specifically an upper body injury. [01:05]
- Building prediction models generally takes 3 to 5 years of data, and Sparta has about seven years across MLB, NFL, NCAA and several countries. [03:36] [04:07]
- The jump was chosen because other tests (sprinting, agility, throwing, hitting, single-leg jumps) are less reliable. [09:05]
- The jump is split into load (standing to squat), explode (how quickly the athlete comes out of the bottom) and drive (how well the movement is prolonged); each is tied to success in different positions or sports. [09:05] [09:36]
- The three scores form a "movement signature," expressed as a t-score where 50 is average. [10:06] [10:39]
- Plates and vertical jumps are not new; what is new is thresholds for what is meaningful. [10:39]
- In one pitcher case, a particular uneven pattern (a "healthy imbalance") is associated with ground ball percentage, and Stanford School of Medicine and BYU statistics are said to have validated it. [11:10]
- A minor league pitcher had rising drive without matching load and then tore his UCL; a publication is said to show drive rising without load predicts severe elbow injury. [12:43] [13:13]
- The plan starts with the lowest variable, then the next one if it is far enough from the others, then left/right differences, recovery, nutrition, hydration and sleep. [13:45] [14:15]
- Being digital is not the same as being scientific. [14:51]
- The program knows where an athlete will be 14 days after a given squat prescription, and general managers call to ask how long until risk is reduced. [15:21]
- Previous injury is the biggest predictor of any injury, and recent sport load adds risk. [16:24] [16:54]
- Organizations can decrease injuries 10 to 20% each year. [17:24]
- Sleep is entered subjectively on a phone app, and the speaker says entries can vary depending on whether contracts are guaranteed. [19:52]
- Sparta is a database company, not a force plate company; other biomarkers are a future area. [20:23]
- A left versus right balance test (eyes closed is more reliable) and a single-leg landing test serve return to play when jumping is not possible. [21:29] [22:31]
- Prior injury is added as a covariate in the predictive model, with decision trees run by statistics partners. [24:05] [24:37]
- The test is physical and removes skill, so it shows whether an athlete needs more skill work or more physical work. [26:42] [27:12]
- Exercises can push a variable the wrong way: squat has the largest effect on load and is the biggest negative detractor of drive. [28:16] [28:49]
- Position affects loading, but movement patterns are shared by skill type across sports. [29:20]
- The system cannot replace discussion; a subjective flag should prompt a conversation with the athlete. [29:52] [30:23]
- Organizations that are most transparent, for example athletes reviewing data within 24 hours, see more buy-in. [31:40]
- The test is not blind; variables are averaged across trials; only load shows a learning effect, which can expose pain or soreness. [32:19] [32:50]
- In baseball the largest prediction target is Tommy John UCL injury (four years of weekly MLB assessments); in the NFL it is a foot injury (caption "Liz Frank," probably Lisfranc, caption spelling), then ACL. [34:05] [34:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Predict 99 injuries" for an MLB team in 2014 [04:07]. The captions give no denominator or percentage and may be garbled. Not usable as stated.
- "$22.5 million" then "$225 million" of predicted season savings [04:39]. The two figures conflict in the captions; I cannot tell which is correct.
- MLB lost over $700 million to injury in 2014. [05:12]
- Seven years of data [03:36]; 3 to 5 years to build prediction models [04:07].
- Portable force plate weighing about 40 pounds. [08:33]
- T-score: a scaled, more accurate percentile; 50 is average. [10:06] [10:39]
- Drive "more than 15 from the others" is the flag tied to severe elbow injury [13:13]; the captions give no unit. The second-variable check is "more than five" [13:45]; the following words ("only one way") are garbled.
- Squat at 80% of bodyweight for five sets of five leads to a known state at 14 days. [15:21]
- Pitch count over the last 30 days more than two standard deviations above the athlete's normal. [16:54]
- Claimed injury reduction of 10 to 20% per year. [17:24]
- Balance test: 20 seconds, two on each side; left/right t-score of 48 to 51 shown as typical, below 40 is a large risk increase, a left/right difference of 10 is a large injury increase. [21:29] [23:04]
- Four years of weekly MLB assessments. [34:35]

## Methods and frameworks named

- Vertical jump on a portable force plate with a standardized warm-up and set number of trials. [07:48]
- Load, explode and drive scores combined into a movement signature and t-scores. [09:36] [10:06]
- Thresholds built from an anonymous aggregated database of high school, college and professional athletes. [04:07] [10:39] [25:07]

- Would other body chemistry data be added? Yes, as a future area. [20:23]
- How does the left versus right balance test work? Shown with a return-to-play example. [21:29]

- Individual sports? Mostly track and field so far, plus NBA and Kansas basketball. [25:37]
- In-game wearables, skill versus physical? The test removes skill. [26:42]
- Negative effects of exercises? Squat raises load but lowers drive. [28:16]
- Positions? Loading differs; movement is shared by skill type. [29:20]
- Subjective variables? Not correlated yet; they should prompt a discussion. [29:52]
- Player buy-in? Transparency, such as reviewing data within 24 hours. [31:09]
- Is the test blind, can it be cheated? Not blind; averaged; load is sensitive to pain. [32:19]
- Future of Sparta? Help organizations prioritize their time. [33:35]
- What is predicted in each sport? UCL in baseball; foot then ACL in the NFL. [34:05]

## Where this applies

- Inference: Map the talk's load, explode and drive phases onto the driver and strategy metrics Applied Performance already reads from ForceDecks countermovement jumps (for example braking and propulsive phase metrics and phase durations), and check whether any phase-imbalance pattern separates football position groups.
- Inference: Use a single-leg landing and balance benchmark, compared with each athlete's own preseason baseline, as one late-stage return-to-play data point shared with Athletic Medicine.
- Inference: Flag a GPS session or four-week block when an athlete's load sits more than two standard deviations above his own rolling baseline, as a prompt for a conversation, not an automatic restriction.
- Inference: Record prior injury history as a covariate whenever a force plate or GPS flag is reviewed, since the speaker calls previous injury the biggest predictor.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing was chosen as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable, and wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them. The talk agrees on the force plate as the core tool and on the weakness of self-reported sleep (the speaker says entries vary with contract status [19:52]).
- Eric's baseline: metric selection follows output, driver and strategy metrics (Hawkin Dynamics' framework). The talk extends this with a three-phase signature but gives no sample to show it beats that approach.
- Eric's baseline: testing must be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). The talk agrees: it standardized warm-up and number of trials. [07:48]
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric; no sport-specific load thresholds exist yet. The talk conflicts on wording ("predict" injuries) and offers thresholds without showing their evidence.
- Eric's baseline: daily subjective surveys are kept in return to play. The talk agrees that subjective flags should start a conversation. [30:23]

## What would have to be true

- Enough Baylor football CMJ history (several seasons, consistent protocol) to compute individual and position-group baselines.
- Injury records from Athletic Medicine with dates and mechanism, so non-contact injuries can be separated from contact injuries.
- A sample large enough to see any pattern; one team's single-season injuries are likely too few.
- Evidence, from Baylor data or independent studies, that a flagged phase pattern precedes injury more often than chance. The talk shows none.

## Do not apply when

- Baseball pitcher findings (UCL, drive without load) are carried into football; the speaker says football models are younger. [34:35]
- The vendor's thresholds (t-score 40, difference of 10, drive 15 from others) are used without local data or known units.
- The decision would restrict an athlete based on a single flag with no conversation or medical input.
- The number of injuries is too small to tell a signal from noise.
- The 10 to 20% reduction or savings figures are used to justify spend; the captions do not support them.

## First step

Pull one position group's preseason ForceDecks CMJ data, compute each athlete's own baseline and standard deviation, and list last year's non-contact injuries from Athletic Medicine beside it as a read-only, retrospective look. Change nothing in the current workflow.

- Inference: Use a single-leg landing and balance benchmark, compared with each athlete's own preseason baseline, as one late-stage return-to-play data point shared with Athletic Medicine.
- Inference: Flag a GPS session or four-week block when an athlete's load sits more than two standard deviations above his own rolling baseline, as a prompt for a conversation, not an automatic restriction.
- Inference: Record prior injury history as a covariate whenever a force plate or GPS flag is reviewed, since the speaker calls previous injury the biggest predictor.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing was chosen as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable, and wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them. The talk agrees on the force plate as the core tool and on the weakness of self-reported sleep (the speaker says entries vary with contract status [19:52]).
- Eric's baseline: metric selection follows output, driver and strategy metrics (Hawkin Dynamics' framework). The talk extends this with a three-phase signature but gives no sample to show it beats that approach.
- Eric's baseline: testing must be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). The talk agrees: it standardized warm-up and number of trials. [07:48]
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric; no sport-specific load thresholds exist yet. The talk conflicts on wording ("predict" injuries) and offers thresholds without showing their evidence.
- Eric's baseline: daily subjective surveys are kept in return to play. The talk agrees that subjective flags should start a conversation. [30:23]

## What would have to be true

- Enough Baylor football CMJ history (several seasons, consistent protocol) to compute individual and position-group baselines.
- Injury records from Athletic Medicine with dates and mechanism, so non-contact injuries can be separated from contact injuries.
- A sample large enough to see any pattern; one team's single-season injuries are likely too few.
- Evidence, from Baylor data or independent studies, that a flagged phase pattern precedes injury more often than chance. The talk shows none.

## Do not apply when

- Baseball pitcher findings (UCL, drive without load) are carried into football; the speaker says football models are younger. [34:35]
- The vendor's thresholds (t-score 40, difference of 10, drive 15 from others) are used without local data or known units.
- The decision would restrict an athlete based on a single flag with no conversation or medical input.
- The number of injuries is too small to tell a signal from noise.
- The 10 to 20% reduction or savings figures are used to justify spend; the captions do not support them.

## First step

Pull one position group's preseason ForceDecks CMJ data, compute each athlete's own baseline and standard deviation, and list last year's non-contact injuries from Athletic Medicine beside it as a read-only, retrospective look. Change nothing in the current workflow.

The panelists spend most of the hour on four questions: how to set up an organization so data is actually used, how much positional value should drive the draft and free agency, whether trading down is a good bet, and how to think about quarterbacks probabilistically. The recurring argument is that data helps most when it is built into the scouting process from the start, when a team uses its own models and its own history rather than a league-wide rule, and when decisions are made before need and job pressure distort grades. ## Where this applies

- Inference: Cut a recurring coach-facing report (weekly GPS or force plate summary) to a fixed short list of items per group, the way the panel cut about 50 opponent tendencies to a top ten so players could act on it [06:45]. The decision is which few metrics go on the page each week.
- Inference: Treat recruiting grades the way the panel treats scout grades: define vague terms before they are used, and audit each grader's accuracy by position after outcomes are known [35:01], [44:18]. This applies to how PFF-based and staff grades are combined in recruiting grading.
- Inference: For speed evaluation, check whether the flying segment (for example the 30 to 40 yard split or max velocity on GPS) separates athletes better than total 40 time, as the panel claims for receivers [36:34]. The decision is which speed metric goes in a position profile.
- Inference: Run a short process-versus-outcome review of return-to-performance and load decisions (was the call sound given what was known, separately from how it turned out) to avoid judging decisions only by results [13:56].
- Inference: Compare tracked practice exposure (plays or GPS load) against a planned cap per athlete, as the panel did with a play cap [45:50]; Baylor has GPS data to do this more finely.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories beats an exhaustive battery, and data collection is judged on cost versus insight (method-baseline, Testing and Philosophy sections). The talk agrees with cutting to the few items that matter.
- Eric's baseline: 0 to 10 m is read as an acceleration score and 30 to 40 m as a speed score, with 40 m peak velocity derived from the 30 to 40 split (AP Assessment Manual V12, author uncertain, possibly legacy). The talk's flying-20 claim is consistent with reading the later split separately; it extends, it does not conflict.
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and progressions are smooth and gradual (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk's "moving the needle, not certainty" framing agrees [14:28].
- Eric's baseline: early GPS and load monitoring bred a culture of fear that pushed teams toward under-training (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk's play caps [45:50] sit in tension with this: a cap can protect or can under-prepare, so the talk is not evidence that lower exposure is better.
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine decisions rather than making them. The talk's designated upstairs analyst [10:53] is a similar supporting role.

## What would have to be true

- Report trimming: coaches must agree which decisions the report serves, and you need a few weeks of the current report to see which items were used.
- Grader audit: enough graded recruits with known later outcomes at each position to see anything; a handful per position will not show grader skill.
- Flying-split check: a same-athlete sample with both total and split times (and GPS max velocity) and some performance outcome to compare to; the panel showed no data for its claim.
- Process review: a written record of what was known at decision time, kept before the outcome.
- Exposure cap: a defined cap per position and session type, agreed with Athletic Medicine and coaches.

## Do not apply when

- The point is about NFL contracts, dead money, draft value charts or the rookie scale [24:48], [29:21]. College has none of these mechanisms in the same form, so do not port the cap arguments.
- The panel's 2012 NFL view of GPS (it did not work with pads and contact) is one team's experience from then; do not use it to rule GPS out today [45:50].
- A receiver flying-20 claim rests on the panelist's assertion and NFL combine data; do not apply it to college positions, non-receivers or one team's small sample.
- A play cap would under-prepare athletes if set without regard to role and session type (see baseline above).
- Intangible grades can be confounded by outcome: the speaker warns that memorable successes (for example Tebow) hide forgotten failures [43:15].

## First step

Take one existing weekly report and draft a version with only the top three metrics per position group; show it to one coach next to the current one and record which they use. Keep the original.

## Summary

Glenn Fleisig of the American Sports Medicine Institute explains the rise of ulnar collateral ligament (Tommy John) surgery in baseball and what his group's data say about it. He covers the stress on the elbow, how often pitchers return after surgery, risk factors, and prevention. His headline finding: too much pitching, and especially pitching while fatigued, is the strongest risk factor he has found [33:31]. Curveballs were not shown to be more dangerous than fastballs, though he says they were not proven safe [52:31]. He closes with MLB and youth prevention efforts (PitchSmart) and wearable and camera biomechanics tools, some from a company he advises [41:13].

## Key claims

- Professional UCL surgeries were steady for about 20 years, then climbed, so the rise is not a one-year fluke [07:42].
- About 16 percent of professional pitchers have had the surgery, with a higher share among major leaguers that he attributes to more years pitching [08:13], [09:14].
- The ligament has to resist most of the elbow stress in the cocked position, and cadaver work showed the ligament alone cannot take that load, so muscle and other tissue share it [16:28], [17:00].
- The surgery does not improve velocity or performance; he believes the two studies that found performance down toward age-expected levels [21:39], [22:10].
- Return to the majors takes about a year and a half in published studies, about 12 months in his group's data [22:40], [24:15].
- In a spring training comparison, pitchers who had returned from surgery matched never-injured pitchers on flexibility and mechanics [28:21], [28:52].
- Youth pitchers with over 100 competitive innings in a year had over three times the risk of serious elbow or shoulder injury [31:58].
- Retrospective comparisons linked surgery to pitching often when fatigued, pitching many months a year, and high pitch counts in a game [32:30], [33:00].
- Activity in children is polarized: a few do too much, many too little; moderate activity is the goal [36:38], [38:10].
- Lab and field studies did not show curveballs to be more dangerous than fastballs; he advises young pitchers to learn fastball and changeup first [39:41], [40:12], [52:31].
- Fatigue is individual; it cannot be measured in the moment, so coaches and trainers who know the athlete, plus next-day symptoms, are the guide [50:29], [51:30].
- Poor mechanics are shown to increase arm stress, but it is not proven that higher stress causes more injury [58:38].
- Drug-driven muscle gains can outpace ligaments and tendons (his statement, no data shown) [48:54].
- The ultimate goal is tracking pitchers' biomechanics in games, which is not yet available [42:13].

## Numbers and definitions

- Elbow torque in the cocked position: about 100 newton-meters, compared to holding five 12 lb bowling balls on a string [15:27], [15:58]. The clip captions read "512b", which is garbled; 5 x 12 = 60 lb matches [10:45].
- The ligament withstands about 55 percent of the stress, which he gives as 55 newton-meters [16:28].
- Elbow speed 2,300 degrees per second (caption "2,300 de per second") [14:22].
- Elbow about 90 degrees bent at foot contact [14:22].
- Surgeries by age and level: 16 percent of professional pitchers have had it; about 15 percent of minor leaguers and 25 percent of major leaguers [08:13], [08:44]. The 16 percent and 25 percent come from a study he says is not yet published.
- Return rates: about 80 percent return; about 67 percent return and stay [22:10]. His group's rate is about 80 percent, regardless of high school, college or pro [23:11], [56:34].
- Return time: about 18 months in the studies vs about 12 months in his group's data [22:40], [24:15].
- Three published studies: one covering 1974 to 2012, one of 147 pitchers since 1999, one of 38 recent pitchers with PitchFX data since 2008 (caption names "Ericson", "mcne/mockney", "Jang"; spellings unverified) [20:04], [20:35], [21:05].
- Spring training study: 40 post-surgery vs 40 never-injured pitchers, both about 85 mph [25:47], [28:21].
- Youth cohort: about 500 pitchers followed weekly during a season and yearly for 10 years; over 100 innings in any year meant more than three times the risk [31:28], [31:58].
- Odds from retrospective questions: pitching over 80 pitches in a game, 4 to 1; more than 8 months a year, 5 to 1; pitching often when fatigued, 36 to 1 [32:30], [33:00], [33:31]. The "8 months" figure and "$36 to $1" wording are caption-dependent.
- Lab: over 2,000 pitchers tested; 12 cameras, about 40 markers, 500 frames per second (captions say "pictures") [13:20], [43:13].
- Proper mechanics definition: about 150 pitchers tested with healthy arms for at least a year and high fastball velocity; mean and standard deviation of each measure [55:03], [55:33].
- Fastball velocity averaged about 2 mph higher since 2002 and the count of pitchers averaging 94 mph doubled (from a clip in the talk, not Fleisig's own data) [10:15].
- Success after surgery in the studies: at least 10 major league games [53:32], [54:02].
- Latin American pitchers: same rate, about 16 percent [57:05], [57:36].

## Methods and frameworks named

- 3D motion capture lab with reflective markers; kinematics measured, kinetics (forces and torque) calculated from motion [11:46], [12:17].
- Cadaver testing of ligament strength [16:28].
- Case comparison of pitchers with and without surgery on history questions [32:30].
- Prospective youth cohort with weekly and yearly follow-up [31:28].
- Spring training field labs with MLB, four mechanical hypotheses (compensation, holding back, "inverted W", low elbow then raise) [25:47], [26:47], [27:18].
- Reference-range definition of proper mechanics from healthy high-velocity pitchers [55:03].
- MLB elbow task force and the PitchSmart guidelines and risk survey [45:49], [46:19], [46:50].

## Limits and open questions

- Some figures come from unpublished work (16 percent, 25 percent, spring training study at the time) [08:13], [28:21].
- Spring training study: minor leaguers only, measured only after return, and only successes [28:52], [29:22], [29:53]. No pre-injury mechanics.
- Retrospective odds (4 to 1, 5 to 1, 36 to 1) rely on recall, not controlled prospective measures, and he says himself he did not say causation beyond this [32:30], [33:31].
- Proper mechanics is defined by fast velocity and health, so the benchmark is partly circular; in follow-up, poor mechanics predicted injury about half the time, and the link from arm stress to injury is unproven [55:03], [58:38].
- Curveball result: failure to prove danger is not proof of safety, as he says [52:31].
- Long-term outcomes for surgery at young ages are unknown [56:34].
- Institutional and commercial interest: he advises MLB, Little League, USA Baseball and modus, and is helping develop its devices [06:08], [41:13].
- The chair says the talk is on a panel; the clip from another professor on ball pressure is unrelated to the talk [01:31].
- Caption garbles: "thousand pictures" (likely pitchers) [23:11]; "mcne", "mockney", "Ericson", "Jang", "Kane c a i n" unverified; "sa young" is Cy Young, caption spelling [13:51].

## Q&A

- How do you know when a pitcher is fatigued: individual, not measurable in the moment, rely on knowing the pitcher, trainers and next-day symptoms [49:59], [50:29], [51:30].
- Split-finger fastball stress: not studied; fastballs, curveballs and sliders are stressful and changeups less so [52:01], [53:02].
- What counts as return success: the studies used at least 10 major league games; he prefers staying healthy and stats matching age [53:32], [54:02].
- How proper mechanics were determined: healthy, fast pitchers' mean and standard deviation [54:32], [55:33].
- Age at surgery: about 80 percent return across levels; long-term outcomes for the young are unknown [56:03], [56:34].
- Latin American pitchers: same rate as Americans [57:05].
- Did poor-mechanics pitchers get injured: about half did, half did not; arm stress-to-injury link not proven [58:06], [58:38].

## Where this applies

- Inference: If Applied Performance supports baseball, track season and year-round throwing exposure (pitches, innings, months) and fatigue flags per pitcher, because exposure and pitching when fatigued were the strongest risk markers in his data [31:58], [33:31].
- Inference: Build a reference range for a force plate or GPS metric from healthy, high-performing Baylor athletes at a position (mean and standard deviation), as Fleisig did for mechanics [55:33], and use it as a flag, not a verdict.
- Inference: Use the "fatigue is individual; next day matters" rule to shape football practice monitoring: pair daily objective data with trainer and coach knowledge of the athlete [50:29], [51:30].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ replaced subjective wellness surveys as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable; surveys were dropped after athletes gamed them, but kept for return-to-play (Eric's SportSmith article). The talk partly conflicts: Fleisig relies on trainer and athlete next-day report and says fatigue cannot be measured in the moment [50:29]. The baseline keeps subjective input in RTP, which fits his context.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters as much as technology for daily assessment (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees, with trainers as the key reader of fatigue [51:30].
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated; smooth, gradual progression of load (course material, speaker unconfirmed). The talk extends this with overuse and exposure evidence from youth baseball.
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports RTP decisions with information; no RTP criteria are documented in the corpus. The talk offers a multi-part success definition that could fill a gap [54:02].
- Eric's baseline: force plate metrics are chosen by the output, driver, strategy and symmetry framework (Hawkin Dynamics). The talk's reference-range method extends it but does not replace it.
- Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric. No direct link to Fleisig's risk odds beyond this.

## What would have to be true

- Return definition: agreement with Athletic Medicine and coaches on criteria and time windows before any return is judged.
- Age-expected comparison: a comparison group of similar athletes, with enough players per position to estimate a trend.
- Exposure tracking: reliable counts (pitches, innings, months of throwing) from baseball staff; without them the odds cannot be checked.
- Reference ranges: enough healthy athletes at a position, same test protocol every time, and a check that the range predicts something at Baylor.
- Fatigue process: trainers and coaches who see the athlete daily and a written trigger for what happens when they flag him.

## Do not apply when

- The data are pitchers (baseball overhead throwing); do not transfer elbow torque, UCL return rates or pitch-count figures to football or other sports.
- The youth findings (500 pitchers, over 100 innings) are not college-level thresholds; do not set a college innings limit from them.
- The 4 to 1, 5 to 1 and 36 to 1 odds are retrospective and recall-based; do not treat them as causal or as predictive risk scores for an individual.

- Sample sizes are small and partly unpublished (38 pitchers in one study, the spring training work); do not generalize a result from one or two studies.
- Vendor devices shown (motion tools from a company the speaker advises) were not validated in the talk [41:13].

## Summary

Phil Wagner, founder of Sparta Science, argues that a standardized vertical jump on a portable force plate can flag injury risk and physical readiness, including upper body injuries in baseball pitchers. He models the approach on medicine: clinical expertise, athlete input and evidence, plus a standardized assessment. The jump is scored on three phases (load, explode, drive) into a "movement signature" with thresholds, and software turns imbalances into a prioritized exercise plan. Injury history, sport load and sleep sit on a dashboard. The talk is a vendor presentation with case studies and claimed results, but no data tables appear in the captions. The Q&A covers balance and landing tests, buy-in, football versus baseball targets and youth use.

## Key claims

- A jump can predict an injury, specifically an upper body injury. [01:05]
- Building prediction models generally takes 3 to 5 years of data, and Sparta has about seven years across MLB, NFL, NCAA and several countries. [03:36] [04:07]
- The jump was chosen because other tests (sprinting, agility, throwing, hitting, single-leg jumps) are less reliable. [09:05]
- The jump is split into load (standing to squat), explode (how quickly the athlete comes out of the bottom) and drive (how well the movement is prolonged); each is tied to success in different positions or sports. [09:05] [09:36]
- The three scores form a "movement signature," expressed as a t-score where 50 is average. [10:06] [10:39]
- Plates and vertical jumps are not new; what is new is thresholds for what is meaningful. [10:39]
- In one pitcher case, a particular uneven pattern (a "healthy imbalance") is associated with ground ball percentage, and Stanford School of Medicine and BYU statistics are said to have validated it. [11:10]
- A minor league pitcher had rising drive without matching load and then tore his UCL; a publication is said to show drive rising without load predicts severe elbow injury. [12:43] [13:13]
- The plan starts with the lowest variable, then the next one if it is far enough from the others, then left/right differences, recovery, nutrition, hydration and sleep. [13:45] [14:15]
- Being digital is not the same as being scientific. [14:51]
- The program knows where an athlete will be 14 days after a given squat prescription, and general managers call to ask how long until risk is reduced. [15:21]
- Previous injury is the biggest predictor of any injury, and recent sport load adds risk. [16:24] [16:54]
- Organizations can decrease injuries 10 to 20% each year. [17:24]
- Sleep is entered subjectively on a phone app, and the speaker says entries can vary depending on whether contracts are guaranteed. [19:52]
- Sparta is a database company, not a force plate company; other biomarkers are a future area. [20:23]
- A left versus right balance test (eyes closed is more reliable) and a single-leg landing test serve return to play when jumping is not possible. [21:29] [22:31]
- Prior injury is added as a covariate in the predictive model, with decision trees run by statistics partners. [24:05] [24:37]
- The test is physical and removes skill, so it shows whether an athlete needs more skill work or more physical work. [26:42] [27:12]
- Exercises can push a variable the wrong way: squat has the largest effect on load and is the biggest negative detractor of drive. [28:16] [28:49]
- Position affects loading, but movement patterns are shared by skill type across sports. [29:20]
- The system cannot replace discussion; a subjective flag should prompt a conversation with the athlete. [29:52] [30:23]
- Organizations that are most transparent, for example athletes reviewing data within 24 hours, see more buy-in. [31:40]
- The test is not blind; variables are averaged across trials; only load shows a learning effect, which can expose pain or soreness. [32:19] [32:50]
- In baseball the largest prediction target is Tommy John UCL injury (four years of weekly MLB assessments); in the NFL it is a foot injury (caption "Liz Frank," probably Lisfranc, caption spelling), then ACL. [34:05] [34:35]

## Numbers and definitions

- "Predict 99 injuries" for an MLB team in 2014 [04:07]. The captions give no denominator or percentage and may be garbled. Not usable as stated.
- "$22.5 million" then "$225 million" of predicted season savings [04:39]. The two figures conflict in the captions; the correct one cannot be told from the captions.
- MLB lost over $700 million to injury in 2014. [05:12]
- Seven years of data [03:36]; 3 to 5 years to build prediction models [04:07].
- Portable force plate weighing about 40 pounds. [08:33]

## Where this applies

- Inference: Map the talk's load, explode and drive phases onto the driver and strategy metrics Applied Performance already reads from ForceDecks countermovement jumps (for example braking and propulsive phase metrics and phase durations), and check whether any phase-imbalance pattern separates football position groups.
- Inference: Use a single-leg landing and balance benchmark, compared with each athlete's own preseason baseline, as one late-stage return-to-play data point shared with Athletic Medicine.
- Inference: Flag a GPS session or four-week block when an athlete's load sits more than two standard deviations above his own rolling baseline, as a prompt for a conversation, not an automatic restriction.
- Inference: Record prior injury history as a covariate whenever a force plate or GPS flag is reviewed, since the speaker calls previous injury the biggest predictor.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing was chosen as the readiness marker because it is objective, consistent and actionable, and wellness surveys were dropped because athletes learned to game them. The talk agrees on the force plate as the core tool and on the weakness of self-reported sleep (the speaker says entries vary with contract status [19:52]).
- Eric's baseline: metric selection follows output, driver and strategy metrics (Hawkin Dynamics' framework). The talk extends this with a three-phase signature but gives no sample to show it beats that approach.
- Eric's baseline: testing must be repeatable ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April"). The talk agrees: it standardized warm-up and number of trials. [07:48]
- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric; no sport-specific load thresholds exist yet. The talk conflicts on wording ("predict" injuries) and offers thresholds without showing their evidence.
- Eric's baseline: daily subjective surveys are kept in return to play. The talk agrees that subjective flags should start a conversation. [30:23]

## What would have to be true

- Enough Baylor football CMJ history (several seasons, consistent protocol) to compute individual and position-group baselines.
- Injury records from Athletic Medicine with dates and mechanism, so non-contact injuries can be separated from contact injuries.
- A sample large enough to see any pattern; one team's single-season injuries are likely too few.
- Evidence, from Baylor data or independent studies, that a flagged phase pattern precedes injury more often than chance. The talk shows none.

## Do not apply when

- Baseball pitcher findings (UCL, drive without load) are carried into football; the speaker says football models are younger. [34:35]
- The vendor's thresholds (t-score 40, difference of 10, drive 15 from others) are used without local data or known units.
- The decision would restrict an athlete based on a single flag with no conversation or medical input.
- The number of injuries is too small to tell a signal from noise.
- The 10 to 20% reduction or savings figures are used to justify spend; the captions do not support them.

## First step

Pull one position group's preseason ForceDecks CMJ data, compute each athlete's own baseline and standard deviation, and list last year's non-contact injuries from Athletic Medicine beside it as a read-only, retrospective look. Change nothing in the current workflow.

## What would have to be true

- Catapult session tags that reliably separate practice types (for example walk-through versus team period) so load can be compared with game peaks.

- Preseason ForceDecks baselines for each athlete, collected with the same protocol.

- A written list of what evidence counts as "independent" for vendors.

## Do not apply when

- NBA, cricket or rugby findings are carried straight into college football without checking Baylor's contact rules and practice limits.

- Higher practice intensity is added to athletes who are already overloaded or have unresolved injuries.
- Athletes cannot see or question their data, which undercuts the trust the panel describes.
- Fewer than a few seasons of consistent data exist for that position group.

## First step

Write a one-page vendor-intake checklist (research requested, independent validation, reproducibility, data ownership) and use it for the next technology pitch. No data or workflow changes.

## Summary

A five-person NFL panel (two current or former club executives, a club research director, a data-vendor executive, and an ESPN moderator) discusses how data should feed roster construction. The panelists spend most of the hour on four questions: how to set up an organization so data is actually used, how much positional value should drive the draft and free agency, whether trading down is a good bet, and how to think about quarterbacks probabilistically. The recurring argument is that data helps most when it is built into the scouting process from the start, when a team uses its own models and its own history rather than a league-wide rule, and when decisions are made before need and job pressure distort grades. Several panelists stress that NFL job security shortens decision horizons.

## Key claims

Caption note: the captions carry no speaker labels. Claims are attributed to a person only where the speech makes it clear; otherwise they are "a panelist".

- A data group only works if the coaches, scouting directors and GM are involved and willing to drop old ideas; teams stay attached to conclusions from data three or four years old [02:32] [03:02].
- A former GM on the panel calls NFL data "criminally underutilized" and says football people often skip surplus value when they look at free agents [04:34] [05:37].
- The same panelist says older thinking held that every "pillar" position had to be filled, and that a team does not need the best left tackle to win a Super Bowl [06:07].
- A research director says the way to sell research internally is to show it solves a specific problem for a GM, scout or coach, and makes their job easier [06:37] [07:07].
- Positional value depends on the organization, its coaches, its scheme and the direction of the league; panelists disagreed over whether wide receiver is the most important non-quarterback position [09:43] [10:14].
- One panelist prefers to ask which units to make strong and which not to leave weak, not to rank positions by pay [11:46].
- The league copies, so an edge is found before others copy and surplus value disappears once everyone chases the same trend [13:49] [14:51].
- No single position was named as undervalued; one panelist argues the edge is volume at receiver and in the secondary, and another argues for tight end [15:22] [15:52].
- A panelist says some teams attach scores to individual metrics in a scouting "metric tree" without weighting the metrics against each other, and calls that subjective [16:54] [17:24].
- Draft-board grades get inflated when a team needs a position; a panelist describes a grade moved from 59 to 65 the night before the draft [19:59] [20:30].
- If two players are close, take the better player; planning for contracts expiring a year or two out can push a pick more than positional value [21:00] [22:01].
- A former GM says every failed decision of his was driven by intense need [24:34].
- Short GM and coach cycles (two to three years) push teams toward need and short windows; a Rams executive says the Rams' data improved because the same head coach and GM stayed seven years [25:04] [25:36].
- Trading down is supported by the view that teams are overconfident in choosing between two similar players [28:38] [29:08]. A panelist counters that a trade chart is an exchange rate, and selling your own picks cheaply repeatedly works against you [32:15] [32:46].
- A panelist argues great players usually come from the top half of the first round, so a team that needs a difference-maker should not trade back [32:46] [33:17].
- Teams use several trade-value charts but often settle on one common currency in a 30-second call; a Rams executive says if three of five models say go, they go [36:18].
- Quarterbacks: a panelist says there are about thirty starting-caliber quarterbacks but only five to eight a team wants to win with [38:50]. Panelists disagree on whether to keep drafting quarterbacks until one is elite [40:20] [46:25].
- A Rams executive says a team close to winning should go for it, but must be honest about whether it is one player away or two; the Rams' 2017 to 2021 run is cited as the goal [50:00] [51:30].
- A Rams executive says the new CBA over-corrected to overvalue top picks, the league then over-corrected on veteran trades, and the market may swing back [55:34] [56:04].
- A panelist says a team that assumes it will beat the draft base rate without a proven formula of its own will fail [57:36] [58:08].

## Numbers and definitions

- First three positions cost about 90 to 100 million dollars of cap "in today's market" (as captioned) [12:17].
- Top receivers jumped seven to eight million in the prior year [13:49].
- Fifth-year option pickup for picks 23 to 32 "starting to fall below 40 percent down to 30 percent" (captions); the speaker says the players who did well in that range were guards, linebackers and safeties [27:38] [28:08].
- Rams: same head coach and GM for seven years; five or six years of collected data [25:36].
- A 2019 trade example: pick 31 traded back to 61 [29:08].
- Vikings moved from pick 12 to 30; pick 12 versus picks 65 and 66 is described as similar on a surplus-value chart [29:40] [30:10].
- Surplus value: described as value beyond what a player will be paid; no formula is given [30:41].
- Claim that no number one overall quarterback from 2009 through 2018 went to a Super Bowl with his team; the speaker asks the room to check it, so it is unverified [42:20].
- Draft base rates quoted: 50 percent first round, 40 percent, 30 percent, down to 10 to 15 percent for seventh-round picks. The captions do not define "hit" [57:36].
- Stafford trade at "basically 50" percent of what Russell Wilson cost the next year (caption wording; may be garbled) [56:04].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Surplus-value trade charts used alongside the Jimmy Johnson chart; teams run several models and compare them [34:18] [36:18].
- Scouting "metric trees" per position with a scored grade; a pyramidal scouting structure (area to regional to national to GM and head coach) [16:54] [19:29].
- A college-to-pro projection model is named as a coming priority, with thinking about mean outcome and upside [57:05] [57:36].
- Draft board reset the night before the draft; picks planned around contracts expiring in a year or two [19:59] [22:01].

## Limits and open questions

- The panel is opinion and anecdote; no datasets, sample sizes or model results are shown. Many claims rest on one executive's experience at one club.
- A data-vendor executive and a club CEO are on the panel, so some claims (for example, that data is underused) are institutional or commercial views.
- Panelists contradict each other on positional value, on drafting quarterbacks repeatedly, and on trade-down value; the talk does not resolve these.
- The fifth-year option figure and the quarterback Super Bowl claim are stated from memory and not checked on stage.
- Names and terms are garbled in places (see speakers field); numbers above are as captioned.

## Q&A

- Audience question: is it easier to build a roster by drafting or by trading, and which is more cost effective? Answers: it depends on the team; the Rams model was back-end picks plus veterans [52:32] [53:02] [55:34].
- Question read by the moderator: how to balance a player's most likely outcome against the upside, and where probability enters scouting grades? Answers: college-to-pro projection models and base rates by round [56:35] [57:36].

## Summary

Three guests (a former NFL executive, the CEO of a football data company, and the president of the Rams) and an ESPN moderator discuss how NFL front offices have changed. The main threads are why some franchises stay bad, how the GM job has widened into managing many more people, and how analytics gets used when coaches and analysts distrust each other. The guests argue that winning is itself a competitive advantage because it buys time, that analytics works best when built into scouting inputs and not delivered as a separate verdict, and that experience and data should be combined. The talk closes on player load and sleep tracking, AI and virtual reality. Much of it is anecdote from one club and one data vendor.

## Key claims

Caption note: captions carry no speaker labels. Attribution below uses context (the Rams president, the former Patriots executive, the data-company CEO).

- Bill Walsh noted that a handful of plays decide a season, and negative-outlier teams tend to stay the same [01:30].
- The data-company CEO says her company's internal debates split into the scout's experienced eye against what the data shows, and that a cap situation affects supply and demand for a team [02:30] [03:01].
- She says human bias about the "winning formula" shows up as the same mistakes repeated [03:32].
- The former Patriots executive says much of winning and losing comes back to fundamentals such as penalties and turnovers before anything advanced [04:35] [05:06].
- The Rams president says the greatest competitive advantage in sports is winning, because it lets you keep people and refine processes [06:38].
- He says sports has shortened GM time frames and incentivized short-term thinking, and calls building teams "art not science" [07:42] [08:12].
- He says a franchise with established success can make unusual decisions that a struggling franchise could not [08:43].
- He says competitive edges erode quickly because ideas spread among clubs [11:46].
- Moderator: every GM hired since 2022 is under 50 [12:16].
- The former Patriots executive says the biggest change in the GM role is the number of people managed, and the variety of views [13:17] [13:48].
- The Rams president says the Rams split the job into picking players and running the building, and that GMs are rarely trained in leadership or soft skills [14:49] [15:20] [15:52].
- He says failed GMs are not given a second chance the way other executives are [16:53]. The former Patriots executive says several Hall of Fame GMs had rough earlier stints [17:23] [17:56].
- The former Patriots executive says the Patriots kept older, experienced people around [18:26].
- The data-company CEO says her company aims to help GMs work faster with more confidence, for example a trade call answered with history and cap impact in seconds [20:29] [21:00].
- She says an outside vendor can invest over a longer term than a club, including frame-level analytics tied back to film [22:01] [22:33] [23:03].
- The Rams president says analytics works when embedded in scouting profiles before scouts and coaches see them [24:06].
- He says the Rams did not use 40-yard times, used three-cone and other speed measures, and stopped attending the combine five years ago [24:37] [25:08].
- He says trust builds only after two to three years of drafted players succeeding [25:38].
- The former Patriots executive says the hardest part of bringing data to football was insecurity on both sides [26:41] [27:11].
- The Rams president says PFF and similar tools becoming common is "probably for the worst" though it gives cover to ask questions [28:42] [29:12].
- He says a coach may face a fourth-down decision five or six times a year, so a high base rate matters less to that coach [35:49]. He says a decision must be supported with organizational resources to make it work [36:50].
- The former Patriots executive says the largest coaching change he has seen is preparation, including player tracking of load, work and sleep [32:17] [32:47] [33:47].
- The data-company CEO says NFL rules restrict tracking outside the club, and clubs ask players to track sleep for them [37:53].
- On experience versus data: the Rams president says dismissing older or younger staff is a mistake and that debate produces better answers [39:27] [41:29].
- The former Patriots executive says character and leadership are not captured in game tape [42:32].
- Closing: the data-company CEO expects more AI and computer vision, and the panel cites VR preparation for a quarterback and an AI question asked at a retreat [44:35] [45:05] [46:35].

## Numbers and definitions

- Six to ten plays can change a season (Walsh, via the moderator) [01:30].
- 600 years of NFL experience at the data company; the speaker has been in football about eight months [02:30].
- Rams president: 17th year, eight years as a "negative outlier" and eight as a "positive outlier" (his wording) [06:07]; also said 16 years as president [14:18]. Records of three and 13, two and 14, then one and 15 before his arrival and in his early seasons [07:11].
- Scouting budgets: "10 to 15 million do" (caption garbled; probably dollars) per club [11:16].
- Every GM hired since 2022 under 50; of four hired this offseason, two under 40 and one under 35 [12:16]. Unverified; moderator's claim.
- Combine: stopped attending five years ago [25:08].
- Fourth-down base rate "62%" over thousands of plays; the unit (conversion rate or other) is not defined [35:49].
- A 2018 playoff fourth and one, up seven with under eight minutes, is given as an example of a conservative coach going for it [36:19].
- Season length: 16, 17 and "about to be 18" games (as captioned) [32:17].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Analytics baked into scouting profiles and player reviews, so it arrives as an input and not an opinion [24:06].
- Three-cone and other measures of speed used in place of 40 times [24:37].
- Frame-level analytics with probability of events, tied to film; anomaly detection as a prompt to look again [22:33] [23:03].
- Player tracking of load and sleep, limited by league rules [32:17] [37:53].
- A retreat decision run through an AI chatbot; no method is described beyond "asked" (caption: "claw") [46:35].

## Limits and open questions

- No data, sample sizes or outcomes are shown; claims are experience and anecdote.
- The data-company CEO describes her own company's products, and the Rams president describes his club's practices, so these are institutional views.
- The Rams president's own record (eight bad years, eight good) is offered as evidence that winning buys time; it is one club.
- Not using 40 times and skipping the combine are reported without results.
- Captions misspell names (peoli, Lissa, "suer" for the vendor, "Mo rant in", "John idik", "claw") and garble the scouting budget figure.

## Q&A

- Audience question: are older staff stubborn about modern decisions? Answer: dismissing either older or younger people means likely failure; debate is useful [38:54] [39:27].
- Audience question: as analytics grows, does human intuition decline? Answers: character and leadership are not in game tape; combine experience with patterns from data [42:32] [43:02].
- Moderator closing question: what innovation will we be talking about in five years? Answers: AI, computer vision, VR [44:35] [45:05].

## Summary

A closing panel at SSAC25 with two college general managers, one for Stanford football and one for St Bonaventure men's basketball, moderated by an author who says he is here to learn whether there is a book in the subject. The guests describe how their jobs came about, what the job involves, and how college sports money works after NIL and the transfer portal. Topics include a pending legal settlement and a proposed revenue-sharing cap, collectives, recruiting conversations that include money, private equity interest, protecting non-revenue sports, and whether college will "moneyball" teenage recruits. The speakers say the role is still undefined and that they do not know what it will look like in five years.

## Key claims

Caption note: captions carry no speaker labels. Attribution below is "Stanford GM", "St Bonaventure GM" or "moderator" based on context.

- The moderator says the talk is unprepared and he is using it to learn [01:01].
- Stanford GM says he sits atop football and runs it like a pro team president and GM, and believes his is the only structure in college football with a GM above the head coach [02:34].
- He says the university president proposed the role and sees football changing so fast that not keeping up means being left out [03:36] [04:08].
- He had no idea the role would be created; he was seeing GMs appear at other schools, mostly as heads of personnel under a coach [05:10].
- St Bonaventure GM says he is an alum at a school of roughly 1,800 to 1,900 undergraduates, and calls his job "director of survival" [06:11] [07:14].
- He had helped lead the school's collective, then moved to the job from ESPN [08:47] [09:48].
- His job is to serve the coach and players, raise NIL money, build a payroll structure and use his relationships; the coach decides who is on the team [10:50].
- He says his salary cap is a moving target that changes as fundraising changes [12:21]. His recruiting pool is "endless" [13:22].
- Stanford GM says the pending settlement will bring order and a salary cap, and back pay split mostly to football [14:54] [15:26].
- Speakers say collectives will still exist and a third party (Deloitte is named) would police fair market value; deals over a stated threshold must be reported [17:27] [17:57].
- St Bonaventure GM says fair market value numbers are "made up" by everyone and a third party will rule on them [18:59].
- Recruiting conversations include agents, parents and relatives, and include housing asks [20:01] [20:32].
- Stanford GM says admissions has not lowered standards for football or basketball players and that Stanford's plan is to develop high school recruits, not turn over a third of the roster in the portal [21:02] [28:12].
- St Bonaventure GM says his school cannot win bidding wars, so aims to be a first stop for international players, or a place for players who need a reset, and plans a roster of players 25 and under [24:38] [25:08] [27:10].
- He builds relationships with top high school players who may come back via the portal in two or three years [25:39].
- He treats his cap like an NBA cap, with percentages for top players, mid-level and minimums [27:41].
- Both say replacing a player is typically more expensive than keeping him [29:44].
- Collectives have contracts with players, but players are in effect free agents each year; the extent to which schools can walk away is unknown [30:14] [30:44].
- Stanford GM says football leads revenue and realignment, and supports funding Olympic sports; there is no athletic director at Stanford now, so the president will arbitrate [31:15] [32:46].

## Summary

A five-person NFL panel (two current or former club executives, a club research director, a data-vendor executive, and an ESPN moderator) discusses how data should feed roster construction. The panelists spend most of the hour on four questions: how to set up an organization so data is actually used, how much positional value should drive the draft and free agency, whether trading down is a good bet, and how to think about quarterbacks probabilistically. The recurring argument is that data helps most when it is built into the scouting process from the start, when a team uses its own models and its own history rather than a league-wide rule, and when decisions are made before need and job pressure distort grades. Several panelists stress that NFL job security shortens decision horizons.

## Key claims

Caption note: the captions carry no speaker labels. Claims are attributed to a person only where the speech makes it clear; otherwise they are "a panelist".

- A data group only works if the coaches, scouting directors and GM are involved and willing to drop old ideas; teams stay attached to conclusions from data three or four years old [02:32] [03:02].
- A former GM on the panel calls NFL data "criminally underutilized" and says football people often skip surplus value when they look at free agents [04:34] [05:37].
- The same panelist says older thinking held that every "pillar" position had to be filled, and that a team does not need the best left tackle to win a Super Bowl [06:07].
- A research director says the way to sell research internally is to show it solves a specific problem for a GM, scout or coach, and makes their job easier [06:37] [07:07].
- Positional value depends on the organization, its coaches, its scheme and the direction of the league; panelists disagreed over whether wide receiver is the most important non-quarterback position [09:43] [10:14].
- One panelist prefers to ask which units to make strong and which not to leave weak, not to rank positions by pay [11:46].
- The league copies, so an edge is found before others copy and surplus value disappears once everyone chases the same trend [13:49] [14:51].
- No single position was named as undervalued; one panelist argues the edge is volume at receiver and in the secondary, and another argues for tight end [15:22] [15:52].
- A panelist says some teams attach scores to individual metrics in a scouting "metric tree" without weighting the metrics against each other, and calls that subjective [16:54] [17:24].
- Draft-board grades get inflated when a team needs a position; a panelist describes a grade moved from 59 to 65 the night before the draft [19:59] [20:30].
- If two players are close, take the better player; planning for contracts expiring a year or two out can push a pick more than positional value [21:00] [22:01].
- A former GM says every failed decision of his was driven by intense need [24:34].
- Short GM and coach cycles (two to three years) push teams toward need and short windows; a Rams executive says the Rams' data improved because the same head coach and GM stayed seven years [25:04] [25:36].
- Trading down is supported by the view that teams are overconfident in choosing between two similar players [28:38] [29:08]. A panelist counters that a trade chart is an exchange rate, and selling your own picks cheaply repeatedly works against you [32:15] [32:46].

The main threads are why some franchises stay bad, how the GM job has widened into managing many more people, and how analytics gets used when coaches and analysts distrust each other. The guests argue that winning is itself a competitive advantage because it buys time, that analytics works best when built into scouting inputs and not delivered as a separate verdict, and that experience and data should be combined.
